theme: Sound doctrine; prayer; overseers and deacons
readingInstruction: Read 1 Timothy 1:1-3:16. Paul writes to his younger coworker Timothy, who is leading the church in Ephesus. Notice the concern for sound doctrine, the priority of prayer, and the qualifications for overseers and deacons. Read slowly through 3:1-13 and 3:14-16.
settingTheScene: 1 Timothy, 2 Timothy, and Titus are called the Pastoral Epistles because they were written to pastors, Timothy and Titus, for the care of churches. Paul probably wrote 1 Timothy around AD 62 to 64, after his first Roman imprisonment, to Timothy in Ephesus. False teachers were spreading myths and speculations. Paul instructs Timothy on doctrine, worship, leadership, and conduct in “the household of God, which is the church of the living God.”
observation: “The aim of our charge is love that issues from a pure heart and a good conscience and a sincere faith” (1:5).
“The saying is trustworthy and deserving of full acceptance, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the foremost” (1:15).
“Who desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” (2:4).
“For there is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (2:5).
“The saying is trustworthy: If anyone aspires to the office of overseer, he desires a noble task” (3:1).
“Therefore an overseer must be above reproach” (3:2).
“The household of God, which is the church of the living God, a pillar and buttress of the truth” (3:15).
“Great indeed, we confess, is the mystery of godliness” (3:16).
interpretation:
Paul tells Timothy to charge certain persons not to teach different doctrine, nor to devote themselves to myths and endless genealogies, which promote speculations rather than the stewardship from God that is by faith. “The aim of our charge is love that issues from a pure heart and a good conscience and a sincere faith.” Some have wandered away into vain discussion, desiring to be teachers of the law without understanding. The law is good if one uses it lawfully, as pointing out sin. Then Paul gives his testimony: formerly a blasphemer, persecutor, and insolent opponent, he received mercy because he had acted ignorantly in unbelief. “The saying is trustworthy and deserving of full acceptance, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the foremost.” “Foremost” (or chief) is present tense: Paul still sees himself as the chief of sinners. And he received mercy so that Christ might display his perfect patience as an example. A doxology follows: “To the King of the ages, immortal, invisible, the only God, be honor and glory forever and ever.”

In chapter 2, Paul gives priority to prayer: “First of all, then, I urge that supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings be made for all people, for kings and all who are in high positions, that we may lead a peaceful and quiet life, godly and dignified in every way.” This is pleasing to God our Savior, “who desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. For there is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all.” The gospel is for all kinds of people, and there is only one way. The rest of chapter 2 includes instructions for men and women in worship, including verses 11 to 15 on women teaching, which have been interpreted in different ways. Some hold that Paul restricts the office of elder/teacher to men; others hold that the instruction was shaped by the Ephesian situation, with false teaching among some women; many hold that the passage should be read with attention to the creation reference in verses 13 and 14. Christians who honor Scripture land in different places, so a charitable spirit is called for.

Chapter 3 gives the qualifications for overseers (also called elders or pastors) and deacons. “If anyone aspires to the office of overseer, he desires a noble task.” The list is mostly about character: above reproach, the husband of one wife, sober-minded, self-controlled, respectable, hospitable, able to teach, not a drunkard, not violent but gentle, not quarrelsome, not a lover of money, managing his household well, not a recent convert, well thought of by outsiders. Only “able to teach” is a skill. Deacons likewise must be dignified, hold the mystery of the faith with a clear conscience, be tested, and be faithful. We examine this more on Day 811.

The section ends with the purpose: “I am writing these things to you so that, if I delay, you may know how one ought to behave in the household of God, which is the church of the living God, a pillar and buttress of the truth.” And a hymn: “Great indeed, we confess, is the mystery of godliness: He was manifested in the flesh, vindicated by the Spirit, seen by angels, proclaimed among the nations, believed on in the world, taken up in glory.” The center of church life is Christ.
connection: Acts 20:17-38 records Paul’s farewell to the Ephesian elders. Romans 3:19-20 and 7:12 speak of the use of the law. Acts 9:1-19 tells of Paul’s conversion. Ephesians 2:19-22 describes the household of God. Titus 1:5-9 gives parallel qualifications. Acts 6:1-6 describes the first servants. Philippians 1:1 mentions overseers and deacons. 1 Peter 5:1-4 is Peter’s charge to elders. Hebrews 8:6 and 9:15 speak of the mediator. Philippians 2:5-11 is another early hymn.
application:
Pray for the leaders of the world and of your community by name, as verse 2:1-2 commands.

Pray for the pastors and elders of your church as you read 3:1-7. Which quality do you see in them?

Memorize 1:15 and say it to yourself when you are tempted to think you are too far gone or too good to need grace.
prayerPrompts: Thank Jesus for coming to save sinners and for his mercy to you.
Ask him to help you fight the good fight with a good conscience.
Pray for those in authority and the people around you.
